input:
Pervaporation is a membrane separation process in which a liquid feed is brought into contact with one side of a membrane, while a vacuum applied on the other side draws the permeating component through the membrane in the form of a vapour. In order to characterise the performance of the membranes examined in this work, two key indicators are employed throughout. The first of these is the flux, which is defined as the mass of material permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The second is the separation factor, defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, a quantity which is, accordingly, dimensionless in nature. The experiments were conducted using a feed comprising 85 wt% n-butanol in water at a temperature of 60 °C, and the tests themselves were run for 500 h. It should be noted that only one feed composition was investigated, which inevitably places some limits on the extent to which the findings can be generalised.

As far as the results are concerned, the polymer membrane delivered a flux of 1.8 kg m-2 h-1 in combination with a separation factor of 240, although it is worth mentioning that its flux declined by 14% over the course of 500 h, suggesting a gradual deterioration in performance with time. The zeolite membrane, on the other hand, exhibited a somewhat lower flux of 1.1 kg m-2 h-1, albeit alongside a higher separation factor of 320, and its flux remained essentially unchanged over 500 h, within the bounds of measurement error. Taken together, these results point to an inherent trade-off between throughput and selectivity, with the question of long-term stability adding a further dimension to the comparison. This is particularly significant in light of the fact that flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for one and the same membrane, which makes a combined assessment of this kind a valuable contribution to the field.
target:
Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Performance is stated in two quantities. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and is dimensionless. Both membranes were tested on a feed of 85 wt% n-butanol in water at 60 °C, and each test ran for 500 h.

The polymer membrane gave a flux of 1.8 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 240, and its flux fell 14% over the 500 h. The zeolite membrane gave a flux of 1.1 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 320, and its flux was unchanged over the 500 h within measurement error. The polymer membrane therefore leads on flux and trails on separation factor, and it is the only one of the two whose performance moved during the test: the flux advantage that is its reason for selection is the quantity that decayed. The zeolite membrane holds its initial flux at the cost of the lower throughput. A choice between the two rests on whether the duty can accept the lower flux in exchange for the higher separation factor and the stable operation, and that exchange is unfavourable wherever the flux decline continues past the tested duration. Only one feed composition was tested, so the comparison is established at that composition; flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and the stability contrast recorded here is available only because both membranes were held on test for the full duration.
